To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we present a botanical simulation coupled to a physical simulation, and that our system supports user‐controlled biological functions robustly on polygonal meshes.
we have extended the deformable simplical complex (DSC) with temporally coherent texture and surface cracking, and coupled the cambial growth to the stresses introduced in the model.
we present a botanical simulation coupled to a physical simulation of cracking, and we present an adaptive, user‐controlled, topologically correct, and robust simulation of cambial growth.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: (a) a botanical simulation of tree secondary growth, (b) an efficient, adaptive and robust surface cracking algorithm, and (c) a novel user‐control interface to guide the growth and cracking of the tree bark.

the following questions: How can a user‐defined biological growth model be implemented on a surface mesh? Can the user control the growth of a tree? Can we simulate a tree bark that is cracked by the growth of the trunk?
modeling the cambial growth and bark cracking of tree stems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our work is a first attempt at a botanical model of cambial growth and bark cracking.
the proposed approach is a significant contribution to the state‐of‐the‐art of the field.
our system is a novel and robust botanical growth simulation system that supports user‐controlled cambial growth, and that is robustly coupled to physical cracking of the bark.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we present a novel approach for simulating the growth of trees, and the cracking and peeling of their bark.
it is the first time a botanical simulation has been coupled to a physically based cracking simulation.
we present the first user‐controlled cambial growth model, coupled to a physical simulation of bark cracking.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we demonstrate the use of a DSC for a biological growth simulation, and that we can couple this with a physical model of bark cracking.
we demonstrate a robust, adaptive, user‐controllable, and physically plausible system for simulating cambial growth, and its effect on bark cracking, that can be used for artistic purposes.
we can simulate a large range of biological growth behaviors on any surface mesh, and we can couple these behaviors with user‐controlled cracking.
